text.p: Italian clothing giant Benetton on Tuesday announced its long-anticipated purchase of sister company Benetton Sportsystem, marking a radical change in the group's growth philosophy over its 32-year history.

Benetton is buying 57 percent of Benetton Sportsystem from the Benetton family holding company Edizione Holding for 318 billion lire ($182 million), and it will make an offer for the remaining 43 percent by March 31, 1998 with the payment of a further 249 billion lire.

It added in a statement that Benetton Sportsystem had been valued at 560 billion lire, but that Benetton will be paying slightly more for the whole group due to the delayed payment for the second 43 percent stake.
Benetton is 71.3 percent controlled by Edizione with its remaining shares quoted on the Milan bourse, while prior to this deal Benetton Sportsystem was wholly-owned by Edizione.

The stock market had long awaited the deal by the group based in Ponzano in the Veneto region of northeast Italy, but analysts feared that Edizione would inflate the sale price of the loss-making Sportsystem to the cash-rich Benetton.
"From our point of view we have done a good deal, having bought in a moment of weakness," Benetton managing director Carlo Gilardi told a news conference after the announcement.
Benetton Sportsystem had 1996 sales of 1.246 trillion lire in 1996, but registered a net loss 14 billion lire after making a small profit of 25 billion lire in 1995.
Gilardi said Sportsystem was already returning to profit for 1997 and in a couple of years believed it would be reporting operating profit margins in the order of eight percent.

The deal brings together clothing manufacturer Benetton, which sells through its 7,000 licensed retail outlets in 120 countries, with a company with a number of well-known brands such as Rollerblade selling through independent retail outlets.

Analysts said it may be difficult to link Benetton's unique system of manufacturing, commissioning agents and licensed retail outlets with Sportsystem, and said the only real synergies between the two groups would be in branded sportswear.
They said Sportsystem would dilute Benetton's margins and could be seen as a risky move after Benetton's history of steady organic growth, but others said it was a move Benetton needed.

"Benetton needed an acquisition to grow. The sector is mature and it could not repeat the rate of expansion of the last years without an acquisition," said Giulia Archetti analyst at Milan brokers Comit.

Benetton Sportsystem boasts a number of leading sports brands such as Prince tennis racquets, Nordica ski boots, Rollerblade in-line skates, Kastle skis and bicyles, Killer Loop sportswear and Asolo mountain boots.

Gilardi said Benetton's excess cash in 1997 would amount to 350 billion lire and almost all of this would be used to finance the acquisition. After the purchase, Benetton said it will have a debt to equity ratio of under 30 percent.
Total global sales of the combined group will rise to 4.4 trillion lire, and the proportion of its sales from North America rising to around 20 percent of its total.

Benetton has been careful not draw criticism over paying too much for Sportsystems with investment banks Salomon Brothers and SBC Warburg drafted in to give a "fairness opinion" of the operation. This was further to Benetton being advised by Morgan Stanley and Italy's IMI Segeco and Edizione by Goldman Sachs.
The Benetton share price slipped to show a loss of 2.11 percent at 26,300 lire in a slightly firmer Milan bourse.

Gilardi added that 1997 would see a rise in profits similar to that of 1996 when net profits rose 11.5 percent to 246 billion lire, on sales which fell to 2.871 trillion lire from 2.939 trillion lire in 1995. ($1=1,747 lire)
